messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla, a 24-year-old tailor of Middle Eastern descent, was driving home from her shop two years ago on a rainy Los Angeles evening when a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned her sedan at the intersection. She remembers the impact as a deafening crunch of metal, the glass shattering around her with a sound like breaking bones, and her car spinning twice before coming to rest against a light pole. For what felt like an hour but was maybe thirty seconds, Layla was pinned in her seat, unable to move her legs, certain she was about to die. The fire department had to cut the door off to get her out. She suffered a broken clavicle and several deep lacerations, but she walked away physically intact. The same could not be said for the feeling that, ever since that moment, she is never truly safe.

In the weeks following the crash, Layla began to notice that her mind would not let the event stay in the past. Without warning, she would feel the exact terror of being trapped—the hot sting of shattered glass on her neck, the smell of coolant, the jolt of the truck hitting her door—as if she were still inside the car. The memory of the crash played over and over like a film she could not turn off, each replay bringing back the same suffocating fear. Whenever she tried to fall asleep, her body would jolt awake; she had to keep one ear tuned for sounds of an impact, because she had come to believe that disaster could strike at any moment. That belief—that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that people are not what they seem—grew stronger with each intrusive flashback. She found herself thinking that she had to be especially careful, because you never know what can happen next. That belief made her feel perpetually on edge, as if danger were lurking just out of sight, ready to strike at any moment.

This sense of constant vigilance shaped how Layla managed her daily life. At the tailoring shop, she insisted on working at a table with her back to a wall, where she could see the entire room and every customer who walked in. She scanned faces for signs of threat, rehearsing worst-case scenarios in her head—what she would do if a customer suddenly lunged, if a car crashed through the storefront. Mentally running through these scenarios felt like the only way to be prepared. The more she rehearsed, the more vivid the memory of the crash became: she would see the truck’s grille filling her window, hear the screech of brakes, and her chest would tighten. In turn, each intrusive memory fed her need to check the room again. She had stopped driving entirely and avoided being a passenger in any vehicle. Taking the bus was out of the question—too many cars, too little control. Instead, she walked everywhere, even in cold rain, telling herself that at least on foot she could see danger coming before it hit her. But because she never stayed in a situation long enough to discover it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed—the threat remained as high as the day it was set, as if the crash had happened just yesterday.

Layla’s hypervigilance did not end when she got home. She checked the locks on her apartment three times before bed, kept a clear line of sight to the door, and slept facing the room. When she lay down, she could not let her guard down; the slightest creak of the building made her heart race and conjured the memory of metal grinding against metal. This pervasive fear gradually convinced her that the world was fundamentally hostile, that her vigilance was not a choice but a necessary response to a danger that would never truly leave. The more she scanned her environment for signs of danger, the more evidence she found that the world was unsafe—a stranger’s glance held a hidden intent, a distant siren meant an approaching threat. This only reinforced her conviction that she could trust no one, not even the neighbors she had known for years.

The cycle tightened. Layla’s constant vigilance confirmed her negative appraisals, and those appraisals demanded even more scanning. Preparing for the worst made the memory of the crash feel more imminent, and that feeling of immediacy made her dread the next time she might have to step onto a street. She stopped attending family gatherings because they required a ride from her brother, and her mother began to worry that Layla was disappearing into herself. At work, her boss noticed she flinched every time a delivery truck passed the shop window. Layla told herself she just needed to be more careful, but the truth was that she was exhausted—running a mental threat simulation all day left her drained, yet too wired to sleep.

After two years, Layla finally came to a counseling center because she had canceled a wedding dress fitting for a client, making an excuse about a headache when really she had been too afraid to walk the five blocks to the fabric store. In the intake session, she said what she most feared was that this feeling would never go away—that she would spend the rest of her life looking over her shoulder, trapped inside the memory of that crash. But she also admitted, quietly, that she was tired of being afraid.
